name: Code of Ur-Nammu
what: The oldest surviving law code, from Ur: fixed fines in silver for injuries rather than revenge.
why: Shows that by 2100 BCE kings claimed to rule by published rules, three centuries before Hammurabi.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Code of Ur-Nammu

name: Code of Hammurabi
what: 282 laws carved on a basalt stele: "an eye for an eye" between equals, but fines for harming commoners or slaves.
why: The best-known ancient code; it wrote social rank into law, with different penalties for nobles, commoners and slaves.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Code of Hammurabi

name: Hittite laws
what: About 200 laws that replaced many death penalties with compensation, revised over centuries.
why: An early case of a state softening its own law code on purpose.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Hittite laws

name: Draco's code
what: Athens' first written laws, famously harsh, taking homicide out of the hands of feuding families.
why: Writing law down took it away from aristocratic judges who had kept it in their heads.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Draco (lawgiver)

name: Solon's reforms (seisachtheia)
what: Cancelled debts and banned enslaving Athenian citizens for debt; freed those already enslaved.
why: Slavery stayed legal for foreigners, so Athens became a citizen democracy built on imported slaves.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Seisachtheia

name: Reforms of Cleisthenes
what: Reorganised citizens into ten tribes, created the Council of 500 chosen by lot and gave the Assembly sovereignty.
why: The founding act of Athenian democracy.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Cleisthenes

name: Twelve Tables
what: Rome's first written law, posted in the Forum after plebeians demanded to know the rules patricians judged by.
why: The root of Roman law, and so of civil law across Europe and Latin America.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Twelve Tables

name: Reforms of Shang Yang
what: Legalist reforms in Qin: harsh published laws, collective punishment, ranks for military merit, abolition of hereditary privilege.
why: Built the state machine that let Qin unify China in 221 BCE.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Shang Yang

name: Cyrus Cylinder
what: Cyrus announces he restored temples and let deported peoples go home after taking Babylon.
why: Often called the first charter of human rights, which overstates it: it is royal propaganda, but it records a real policy of letting subjects keep their gods.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Cyrus Cylinder

name: Edicts of Ashoka
what: Rock Edict XII asks subjects to honour all sects, and Ashoka funds Buddhist, Jain and Ajivika ascetics alike.
why: The earliest state policy of toleration carved for the public to read.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Edicts of Ashoka

name: Edict of Milan
what: Constantine and Licinius granted Christians and everyone else freedom to worship and returned seized church property.
why: Ended the persecution of Christians and opened the way to a Christian empire.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Edict of Milan

name: Edict of Thessalonica
what: Theodosius I made Nicene Christianity the state religion and branded other Christians heretics.
why: From here pagan cults and rival Christian groups were progressively banned.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Edict of Thessalonica

name: Theodosian Code
what: A compilation of imperial laws since Constantine, issued in both halves of the empire.
why: The form in which Roman law reached the Germanic kingdoms of the West.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Codex Theodosianus

name: Salic law
what: Clovis had Frankish customary law written in Latin: wergild payments for every injury and killing.
why: Its rule against women inheriting land was later used to bar women from the French throne.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Salic law

name: Corpus Juris Civilis
what: Justinian's commission compiled Roman law into the Code, Digest and Institutes (529 to 534).
why: Rediscovered at Bologna around 1070, it became the basis of law in most of continental Europe.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Corpus Juris Civilis

name: Imperial examinations begin
what: Emperor Yang of Sui set written examinations for the jinshi degree.
why: For 1,300 years most Chinese officials were chosen by exam, a model later copied in Korea, Vietnam and Britain.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Imperial examination

name: Tang Code
what: 502 articles combining Legalist penalties with Confucian family ethics; revised in 653.
why: The model for law codes in Japan, Korea and Vietnam, and in China until 1911.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Tang Code

name: Taiho Code
what: Japan's ritsuryo code, copied from the Tang: ministries, ranks, land allotment and penal law.
why: Created the bureaucratic Japanese state of the Nara period.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Taiho Code

name: Gwageo examinations in Korea
what: King Gwangjong adopted Chinese-style civil examinations on the advice of the Chinese scholar Shuang Ji.
why: A check on the great clans; the exams lasted until 1894.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Gwageo

name: Russkaya Pravda
what: The first law code of the Rus, attributed to Yaroslav the Wise: limited blood feud, fixed fines.
why: The basis of East Slavic law for centuries.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Russkaya Pravda

name: Magna Carta
what: Barons forced King John to accept that no free man could be imprisoned except by lawful judgment, and no tax raised without counsel.
why: Annulled within weeks and reissued many times, it became the symbol of a ruler bound by law.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Magna Carta

name: Golden Bull of 1222
what: Andrew II granted Hungarian nobles freedom from arbitrary arrest and the right to resist the king.
why: Hungary's Magna Carta, seven years after England's.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Golden Bull of 1222

name: Kouroukan Fouga
what: Oral tradition says Sundiata Keita's assembly set the duties of each clan and rules of the Mali Empire.
why: Known only from griots' oral tradition written down in the 20th century, so its text is not reliable evidence for 1236.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Kouroukan Fouga

name: Siete Partidas
what: Alfonso X's seven-part code drawing on Roman law, including rules on slavery that later shaped Spanish America.
why: Remained in force in parts of the Americas, including Louisiana, into the 19th century.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Siete Partidas

name: Great Ming Code
what: The Hongwu Emperor's final code of 460 articles.
why: Adopted almost unchanged by the Qing, it governed China until 1911.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Great Ming Code

name: Alhambra Decree
what: Ferdinand and Isabella ordered all Jews to convert or leave Castile and Aragon within four months.
why: Perhaps 40,000 to 100,000 left, founding Sephardic communities from Morocco to the Ottoman Empire.

name: New Laws of the Indies
what: Charles V banned enslaving Native Americans and limited encomiendas, after Las Casas' campaign.
why: Indigenous slavery was formally banned, but demand for labour shifted to enslaved Africans.

name: Peace of Augsburg
what: Each prince of the Holy Roman Empire could choose Catholicism or Lutheranism for his lands (cuius regio, eius religio).
why: Toleration between rulers, not for subjects; Calvinists were left out, which helped cause the Thirty Years' War.

name: Akbar abolishes the jizya
what: Akbar ended the poll tax on non-Muslims; later he promoted sulh-i kul, "peace with all".
why: Brought Hindu Rajput nobles into the Mughal state as partners.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Akbar

name: Warsaw Confederation
what: The Polish-Lithuanian nobility promised never to shed blood over differences of religion.
why: Europe's first legal guarantee of religious peace, while France was in its Wars of Religion.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Warsaw Confederation

name: Hideyoshi bans the slave trade
what: Toyotomi Hideyoshi ordered an end to Portuguese buying of Japanese people as slaves.
why: One of the first bans on exporting slaves, aimed at foreign traders.

name: Edict of Nantes
what: Henry IV granted French Protestants freedom of worship in set places and about 150 fortified towns.
why: Ended the French Wars of Religion.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Edict of Nantes

name: Tokugawa ban on Christianity
what: Christianity was outlawed and missionaries expelled; persecution followed.
why: Led to the closed-country (sakoku) policy and the hidden Christians of Nagasaki.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Anti-Christian edicts in Japan

name: Law Code of 1649 (Sobornoye Ulozheniye)
what: Abolished the time limit for recovering runaway peasants, binding peasants and their heirs to their lords forever.
why: The legal birth of full Russian serfdom, which lasted until 1861.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Sobornoye Ulozheniye

name: Aurangzeb reimposes the jizya
what: The poll tax on non-Muslims, abolished by Akbar 115 years earlier, was brought back.
why: Alienated Rajput and Maratha allies as the empire overstretched.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Aurangzeb

name: Habeas Corpus Act
what: Anyone held in prison could demand to be brought before a judge to test whether the detention was lawful.
why: The core legal protection against arbitrary arrest in the common-law world.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Habeas Corpus Act 1679

name: Code Noir
what: Louis XIV's decree regulating slavery in French colonies: slaves were movable property, required to be Catholic; punishments set by law.
why: Gave colonial slavery a full legal code in the French empire.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Code Noir

name: Edict of Fontainebleau
what: Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes and ordered Protestant churches destroyed.
why: About 200,000 Huguenots fled to England, the Netherlands, Prussia and the Cape, taking their skills with them.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Edict of Fontainebleau

name: Bill of Rights
what: The crown could not suspend laws, raise taxes or keep an army in peacetime without Parliament.
why: Made England a parliamentary monarchy; a model for the US Bill of Rights.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Bill of Rights 1689

name: Toleration Act
what: Protestant dissenters could worship in their own chapels; Catholics and non-Trinitarians were still excluded.
why: Partial toleration: dissenters still could not hold office until 1828.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Toleration Act 1688

name: Serfdom Patent
what: Joseph II let serfs in Bohemia and Austria marry, move and learn trades without the lord's consent; labour dues remained.
why: Ended personal bondage but not the robot (labour service), which lasted until 1848.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Serfdom Patent (1781)

name: United States Constitution
what: A written frame of government with separated powers, ratified in 1788; it counted enslaved people as three-fifths for representation.
why: The oldest written national constitution still in use.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Constitution of the United States

name: August Decrees
what: The National Assembly abolished feudal privileges, tithes and the remaining personal servitude in France.
why: Wiped out the legal basis of the old order in one night (4 August 1789).

sources.cite: Wikipedia: August Decrees

name: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
what: Men are born free and equal in rights; sovereignty belongs to the nation; law is the expression of the general will.
why: Its universal language was quickly turned by women and enslaved people against its own limits.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

name: First Amendment
what: Congress may make no law establishing a religion or prohibiting its free exercise.
why: Separated church and state at the federal level; some states kept established churches until 1833.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: First Amendment to the United States Constitution

name: Danish ban on the slave trade
what: Denmark-Norway decreed an end to its transatlantic slave trade, taking effect in 1803.
why: The first European state to ban the trade.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Danish slave trade

name: France abolishes slavery
what: The National Convention abolished slavery in all French colonies, ratifying the Saint-Domingue uprising.
why: The first abolition by a major colonial power; Napoleon reversed it in 1802.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Law of 4 February 1794

name: Napoleon restores slavery
what: The law of 20 May 1802 restored slavery and the slave trade in the colonies France had kept.
why: Provoked the final war in Saint-Domingue that created Haiti.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Law of 20 May 1802

name: Napoleonic Code
what: One civil code for all of France: equality before the law, secure property, no feudal privileges, but wives subject to husbands.
why: Spread by conquest and imitation across Europe, Latin America and the Middle East.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Napoleonic Code

name: Constitution of Haiti
what: The first constitution of independent Haiti abolished slavery forever, after the only successful slave revolution.
why: The first state in the Americas to end slavery permanently.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Constitution of Haiti (1805)

name: Slave Trade Act
what: Parliament banned British subjects from the Atlantic slave trade; the Royal Navy later patrolled West Africa.
why: Britain had been the largest slave-trading nation; slavery itself stayed legal in its colonies until 1834.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Slave Trade Act 1807

name: Act Prohibiting Importation of Slaves
what: Banned importing enslaved people into the United States from 1 January 1808, the earliest date the Constitution allowed.
why: The internal slave trade from the Upper South to the cotton frontier grew instead.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Act Prohibiting Importation of Slaves

name: October Edict
what: Stein's edict, issued at Memel after defeat by Napoleon, freed Prussian serfs from hereditary subjection from 1810.
why: Part of the reforms that rebuilt Prussia; peasants still paid lords for land until the 1850s.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Stein-Hardenberg reforms

name: Constitution of Cadiz
what: Written by the Cortes during the French occupation: a constitutional monarchy with near-universal male suffrage.
why: Abolished by Ferdinand VII in 1814, but copied across Europe and Latin America as the liberal model.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Spanish Constitution of 1812

name: Chile abolishes slavery
what: After a free-womb law in 1811, Chile freed all enslaved people.
why: One of the first abolitions in the independent Americas.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Slavery in Chile

name: Mexico abolishes slavery
what: President Vicente Guerrero, of African and Indigenous descent, decreed abolition.
why: Anglo settlers in Texas resisted it, one cause of the Texas Revolution of 1835 to 1836.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Slavery in Mexico

name: Slavery Abolition Act
what: Abolished slavery in most of the British Empire from 1834, with "apprenticeship" until 1838 and £20 million paid to slave-owners, not to the enslaved.
why: Freed about 800,000 people in the Caribbean, Cape and Mauritius; India was excluded until 1843.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Slavery Abolition Act 1833

name: Edict of Gulhane (Tanzimat)
what: The sultan promised security of life and property, fair trials and regular taxation for all subjects, Muslim or not.
why: Began the Tanzimat reforms and the idea of equal Ottoman citizenship.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Edict of Gulhane

name: Tunisia abolishes slavery
what: Ahmad Bey freed all enslaved people in Tunisia, after closing the slave market in 1841.
why: The first abolition in the modern Muslim world.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Slavery in Tunisia

name: France abolishes slavery again
what: Victor Schoelcher's decree of 27 April 1848 ended slavery in the French colonies for good.
why: Freed about 250,000 people in the Caribbean, Reunion and Senegal.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Abolition of slavery in France

name: Austria abolishes serfdom
what: The revolutionary Reichstag ended labour service (robot) and other feudal dues in the Austrian Empire.
why: The one reform of 1848 the restored monarchy kept.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Revolutions of 1848 in the Austrian Empire

name: Eusebio de Queiros Law
what: Brazil banned importing enslaved Africans, under British naval pressure.
why: Brazil had received about 40 percent of all Africans shipped across the Atlantic.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Eusebio de Queiros Law

name: Northcote-Trevelyan Report
what: Recommended recruiting British civil servants by competitive exam; in force from 1870.
why: Its authors cited the Chinese examination system as a model.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Northcote-Trevelyan Report

name: Emancipation Reform
what: Alexander II freed about 23 million privately owned serfs, who had to pay redemption for their land over 49 years.
why: The largest single emancipation in history; land debts and village communes left peasants poor.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Emancipation reform of 1861

name: Emancipation Proclamation
what: Lincoln declared enslaved people in rebelling states free; it did not apply to loyal border states.
why: Made the Civil War a war against slavery and opened the Union army to Black soldiers.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Emancipation Proclamation

name: Netherlands abolishes slavery
what: Slavery ended in Suriname and the Dutch Caribbean, with ten years of forced state supervision after.
why: Owners were compensated; the freed were not.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Abolition of slavery in the Netherlands

name: Thirteenth Amendment
what: Abolished slavery in the United States "except as a punishment for crime".
why: Freed about 4 million people; the crime exception later allowed convict leasing.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution

name: Fifteenth Amendment
what: States could not deny the vote on account of race, colour or previous servitude.
why: Southern states got round it with poll taxes and literacy tests until the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Fifteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution

name: Law of Free Birth
what: Children born to enslaved mothers in Brazil were free, though bound to serve the owner until 21.
why: A gradual path that slaveholders hoped would delay abolition for decades.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Law of Free Birth

name: Ottoman Constitution
what: Created an elected parliament with Muslim and non-Muslim deputies; suspended in 1878.
why: The first constitution in the Muslim world, restored in 1908.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Ottoman constitution of 1876

name: Spain abolishes slavery in Cuba
what: Ended the patronato (forced apprenticeship) of 1880; Puerto Rico had abolished slavery in 1873.
why: Cuba was the last Spanish colony with slavery.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Slavery in Cuba

name: Golden Law (Lei Aurea)
what: Princess Isabel signed a two-article law ending slavery in Brazil without compensation.
why: The last abolition in the Americas; the angry planters helped overthrow the monarchy the next year.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Lei Aurea

name: Meiji Constitution
what: A constitution granted by the emperor, modelled on Prussia, with an elected lower house.
why: The first constitution in Asia that lasted; it left the army answerable only to the emperor.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Meiji Constitution

name: Gabo Reform
what: Abolished the hereditary nobi slave system, class distinctions and the gwageo exams in Korea.
why: Ended a slave system that once held perhaps a third of Korea's population.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Gabo Reform

name: Plessy v. Ferguson
what: The Supreme Court upheld racial segregation under "separate but equal".
why: Gave constitutional cover to Jim Crow laws across the South for 58 years.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Plessy v. Ferguson

name: Siam abolishes slavery
what: Chulalongkorn's Slave Abolition Act completed a phased emancipation begun in 1874.
why: Done gradually to avoid revolt and to keep Siam free of colonial "civilising" claims.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Slavery in Thailand

name: Qing abolishes the imperial examinations
what: The 1,300-year-old examination system was ended in favour of modern schools.
why: Cut the link between gentry and throne; the dynasty fell six years later.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Imperial examination

name: October Manifesto
what: Nicholas II promised civil liberties and an elected Duma with power over laws.
why: Ended the absolute autocracy, though the 1906 Fundamental Laws took much back.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: October Manifesto

name: Persian Constitution
what: Mozaffar ad-Din Shah accepted an elected Majlis after protests by merchants and clergy.
why: The first parliament in the Middle East outside the Ottoman Empire.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Persian Constitution of 1906

name: Qing abolishes slavery
what: A Qing edict banned the buying and selling of people.
why: Bondservant and child-selling practices continued in the countryside for decades.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Slavery in China

name: Nineteenth Amendment
what: States could no longer deny the vote on account of sex.
why: Gave about 26 million women the vote; Black women in the South stayed largely excluded until 1965.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution

name: Enabling Act
what: The Reichstag let Hitler's cabinet make laws, even unconstitutional ones, without parliament.
why: The legal end of the Weimar democracy.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Enabling Act of 1933

name: Nuremberg Laws
what: Stripped German Jews of citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and other Germans.
why: The legal framework for the persecution that led to the Holocaust.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Nuremberg Laws

name: Ethiopia abolishes slavery
what: Haile Selassie's proclamation completed abolition after earlier decrees of 1924 and 1931.
why: Slavery had been a charge used to justify Italy's 1935 invasion.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Slavery in Ethiopia

name: Population Registration Act
what: Classified every South African by race, the basis of apartheid laws on residence, marriage and voting.
why: Repealed in 1991, three years before the first democratic election.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Population Registration Act, 1950

name: Brown v. Board of Education
what: The Supreme Court ruled segregated public schools unconstitutional, overturning Plessy.
why: Began the legal dismantling of Jim Crow.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Brown v. Board of Education

name: Saudi Arabia abolishes slavery
what: Prince Faisal's government abolished slavery and compensated owners.
why: Yemen abolished it the same year.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Slavery in Saudi Arabia

name: Civil Rights Act and Voting Rights Act
what: Banned segregation in public places and employment (1964) and racial barriers to voting (1965).
why: Ended legal segregation in the United States.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Civil Rights Act of 1964

name: Mauritania abolishes slavery
what: The last country to abolish slavery by law; it was made a crime only in 2007.
why: Descent-based slavery is still reported there.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Slavery in Mauritania

name: Repeal of apartheid laws
what: Parliament repealed the Population Registration, Group Areas and Land Acts.
why: Cleared the way for the first election with universal suffrage in 1994.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Negotiations to end apartheid in South Africa
